"**See You Again**" is a song written, produced, and performed by American rapper and producer [Tyler, the Creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler,_the_Creator "Tyler, the Creator") featuring vocals from Colombian-American singer [Kali Uchis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kali_Uchis "Kali Uchis"). It was released as the fourth single from Tyler's fifth studio album _[Flower Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower_Boy "Flower Boy")_ (2017) on August 29, 2017.[\[3\]](#cite_note-:0-3) The single went viral on [TikTok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TikTok "TikTok"),[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) leading the song to enter several charts around the world for the first time as a [sleeper hit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleeper_hit "Sleeper hit") in April 2023.

Tyler, the Creator initially created the instrumental for the song in 2013, with his friend [Hodgy Beats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodgy_Beats "Hodgy Beats") posting a snippet of it via [Vine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vine_\(service\) "Vine (service)"). This song was first recorded during a studio session in 2014 with Kali and Tyler.

Tyler, the Creator originally wrote the song for former [One Direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Direction "One Direction") member [Zayn Malik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayn_Malik "Zayn Malik"), who turned it down. According to Tyler, Malik "flaked on studio time twice" and he kept the song for himself.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

## Commercial performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=See_You_Again_\(Tyler,_the_Creator_song\)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Commercial performance")\]

Upon release, the song peaked at number 13 on the US [Bubbling Under Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubbling_Under_Hot_100 "Bubbling Under Hot 100") and failed to chart on the main [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). However, in April 2023, the song went viral on TikTok, leading to its first ever appearance on the US _Billboard_ Hot 100 at number 65 before the song reached a peak of number 44. It has also been considered Tyler, the Creator's most successful single to date.

The music video was directed by Tyler, the Creator under the alias of Wolf Haley and uploaded on YouTube on August 8, 2018. [ASAP Rocky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASAP_Rocky "ASAP Rocky") makes a cameo to the video, as well as Tyler Baudelaire, the alter ego later used for the promotion of _[Call Me If You Get Lost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_Me_If_You_Get_Lost "Call Me If You Get Lost")_ (2021).

In the opening scene, Tyler gets ready for another workday in the close quarters of an aircraft carrier, putting on a suit and eating breakfast while singing the first verse. Kali Uchis appears far away at sea singing the chorus on a rescue boat with other rowers, who jump off the boat near the end of the verse.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) The second verse shifts to Tyler on the top deck of the military ship, donning a yellow [beret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beret "Beret"), while soldiers walk behind him. The scene also shows him jumping and walking atop the soldier's heads, with [another person covered in shadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_Me_If_You_Get_Lost "Call Me If You Get Lost") singing the pre-chorus while a man plays trumpet behind him. The scene then shifts to a figure covered in a ghost bed sheet, with the eyes poked out and a bucket hat. At the end of the video, the sheet is pulled off revealing the figure being made up of bees which fly towards the screen.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)

_**Chromakopia**_ (stylized in [all caps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_caps "All caps")) is the eighth studio album by the American rapper [Tyler, the Creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler,_the_Creator "Tyler, the Creator"). It was released through [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") on October 28, 2024, serving as the follow-up to _[Call Me If You Get Lost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_Me_If_You_Get_Lost "Call Me If You Get Lost")_ (2021). _Chromakopia_ was written, produced, and arranged by Tyler himself. The album features guest appearances from [Daniel Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Caesar "Daniel Caesar"), [Doechii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doechii "Doechii"), [GloRilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GloRilla "GloRilla"), LaToiya Williams, [Lil Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Wayne "Lil Wayne"), [Lola Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lola_Young_\(singer\) "Lola Young (singer)"), [Santigold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santigold "Santigold"), [Schoolboy Q](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoolboy_Q "Schoolboy Q"), [Sexyy Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexyy_Red "Sexyy Red"), and [Teezo Touchdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teezo_Touchdown "Teezo Touchdown"), with physical releases of the album additionally featuring [Playboi Carti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboi_Carti "Playboi Carti").

The album blends different genres like [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"), [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), and [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), evocative of Tyler's previous releases _[Flower Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower_Boy "Flower Boy")_ (2017) and _[Igor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_\(album\) "Igor (album)")_ (2019). Conceptually, _Chromakopia_ is narrated by Tyler's mother, Bonita Smith, as a [diary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary "Diary") that pieces together Tyler's perspective on past timeline experiences separated by tracks. The album received widespread acclaim from critics, who praised the lyricism, cohesiveness, and production, and even noted its messy and confusing nature as a positive.

_Chromakopia_ was supported by the singles "[Noid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noid_\(Tyler,_the_Creator_song\) "Noid (Tyler, the Creator song)")", "[Sticky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sticky_\(Tyler,_the_Creator_song\) "Sticky (Tyler, the Creator song)")", and "[Like Him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Like_Him "Like Him")", as well as the promotional singles "[St. Chroma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Chroma "St. Chroma")" and "[Thought I Was Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thought_I_Was_Dead "Thought I Was Dead")". The album was a commercial success, debuting at number one in nine countries. In the United States, the album debuted at the top of the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), earning Tyler his third US number-one album. Several other songs from the album also charted on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), such as "Noid" and "St. Chroma". At the [68th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/68th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "68th Annual Grammy Awards"), the album received nominations for [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year"), [Best Rap Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rap_Album "Grammy Award for Best Rap Album") and [Best Album Cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Album_Cover "Grammy Award for Best Album Cover"), in addition to "[Darling, I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darling,_I "Darling, I")" receiving a nomination for [Best Rap Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rap_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance") and "Sticky" for [Best Rap Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rap_Song "Grammy Award for Best Rap Song"). In support of the album, Tyler embarked on [Chromakopia: The World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromakopia:_The_World_Tour "Chromakopia: The World Tour") between February 2025 and March 2026.

## Background and recording

On October 28, 2024, during Tyler, the Creator's _Chromakopia_ exclusive listening event, Tyler revealed the meaning behind the album, noting that the album was originally about him growing up in [Hawthorne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawthorne,_California "Hawthorne, California"), [Inglewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inglewood,_California "Inglewood, California"). He revealed on stage that "no one knows anything about me from before I was like 17" and that the record turned into Tyler "taking a bunch of shit my mom told me as a kid."[\[1\]](#cite_note-Listening_Event_LA-1) Tyler uploaded a video on his official [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel titled "MASK IS OFF: CHROMAKOPIA" on November 12, 2024, which chronicles the creative process of the album, including [behind-the-scenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behind-the-scenes "Behind-the-scenes") clips from composition sessions, instrumentation arrangements and engineering work.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)

## Composition

### Music

Primarily a [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"), [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B"), and [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") album, _Chromakopia_ embraces [eclectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism "Eclecticism") instrumentation.[\[3\]](#cite_note-MEFeater-3) It blends musical styles reminiscent of Tyler's fourth and fifth albums _[Cherry Bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Bomb_\(album\) "Cherry Bomb (album)")_ (2015) and _[Flower Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower_Boy "Flower Boy")_ (2017), such as [neo soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo_soul "Neo soul") melodies and [synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer")\-based arrangements.[\[3\]](#cite_note-MEFeater-3) [Military cadences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_music "Martial music") and [soulful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") elements are also present on the album.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) This is Tyler's first album since his second studio album, _[Goblin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goblin_\(album\) "Goblin (album)")_, to not have the 10th track on the album feature multiple titles and parts.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

### Themes and lyrics

_Chromakopia_ is narrated by Tyler's mother, Bonita Smith.[\[6\]](#cite_note-TLOBF-6) Its [concept](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album") was inspired by his experience growing up in [Greater Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Los_Angeles "Greater Los Angeles") and the life lessons he learned from Smith as a child, that he began to understand and appreciate as he grew older.[\[7\]](#cite_note-Monogamy-7) Before the album's release, publications speculated that the album could be based on the story of Chroma the Great, a powerful [conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conducting "Conducting") whose orchestra creates the colors of the world, from the 1961 children's novel _[The Phantom Tollbooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Phantom_Tollbooth "The Phantom Tollbooth")_.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) _[Dork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dork_\(magazine\) "Dork (magazine)")_'s Jake Hawkes notes the character ties into the album's [aesthetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesthetics "Aesthetics"), but has little impact on the lyrical material.[\[9\]](#cite_note-Dork-9)

Smith describes him as the light and tells him to never dim his light for anyone.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) "[Rah Tah Tah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rah_Tah_Tah "Rah Tah Tah")" features [braggadocious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braggadocio_\(rap\) "Braggadocio (rap)") lyrics, as Tyler declares himself as the biggest rapper from Los Angeles after [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar").[\[9\]](#cite_note-Dork-9) "[Noid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noid_\(Tyler,_the_Creator_song\) "Noid (Tyler, the Creator song)")", on the other hand, explores his anxieties with [celebrity culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_culture "Celebrity culture") and [parasocial relationships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasocial_relationships "Parasocial relationships").[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) In "[Darling, I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darling,_I "Darling, I")", featuring vocals by [Teezo Touchdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teezo_Touchdown "Teezo Touchdown"), Tyler reflects on his artistic ambition and the practice of [monogamy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogamy "Monogamy").[\[7\]](#cite_note-Monogamy-7)

Titled after the [abortion-related healthcare company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey_Jane "Hey Jane"), "Hey Jane" stages a conversation between Tyler and an anonymous, older woman in the wake of an unplanned pregnancy.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_'s Mackenzie Cummings-Grady wrote that on the record, Tyler "speaks on his consuming paranoia" while narrating his "desire for children".[\[13\]](#cite_note-BB_songs_ranked-13)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Chromakopia.png/330px-Chromakopia.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chromakopia.png)

The _Chromakopia_ album logo, using the font Poleno Semi Bold, with horn-like accents

Provoked by [Beyoncé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyoncé "Beyoncé")'s [surprise release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surprise_release "Surprise release") of her [2013 self-titled album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyoncé_\(album\) "Beyoncé (album)"),[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) the [International Federation of the Phonographic Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_the_Phonographic_Industry "International Federation of the Phonographic Industry") (IFPI) changed the day of the week when music is released worldwide from Tuesday to Friday.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) Tyler criticized the industry standard in a 2023 interview with [Nardwuar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nardwuar "Nardwuar"), suggesting that it promotes "passive listening".[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) He chose to release _Chromakopia_ on Monday, October 28, 2024, at 6 a.m. [ET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone").[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)

Trucks and [shipping containers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipping_container "Shipping container") promoting _Chromakopia_ were spotted in various cities across the U.S., including [Tyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler,_Texas "Tyler, Texas"), Houston, Dallas, Atlanta, [Charlotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte,_North_Carolina "Charlotte, North Carolina"), [Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"), Philadelphia, [Roswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell,_New_Mexico "Roswell, New Mexico"), Phoenix, Hawthorne (Tyler's hometown), and Los Angeles.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) Shortly after the video for "St. Chroma" released, the phone number +1 (855) 444–8888, which was previously used as promotion for _Call Me If You Get Lost_, was changed to a voicemail concerning the "Chromakopia Trucking Company", where a voice said that all the company's drivers were unavailable and to call later. One day before its release, Tyler held an album listening party at [Intuit Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuit_Dome "Intuit Dome").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Listening_Event_LA-1)

A deluxe edition of the album, titled _Chromakopia+_, was released on October 29, 2025.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) It includes the bonus track "Mother", which was previously exclusive to the album's vinyl LP release.[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)

### Singles

On October 16, 2024, Tyler posted a teaser for _Chromakopia_'s opening track, "St. Chroma", on his [social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media "Social media") accounts.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) He revealed the album's name, release date, and [cover art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_art "Cover art") the following day.[\[24\]](#cite_note-variety_oct17-24)[\[25\]](#cite_note-25) The album's [lead single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single"), "Noid", was released on October 21.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) The following single, "[Sticky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sticky_\(Tyler,_the_Creator_song\) "Sticky (Tyler, the Creator song)")" featuring [GloRilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GloRilla "GloRilla"), [Sexyy Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexyy_Red "Sexyy Red"), and [Lil Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Wayne "Lil Wayne"), was released to [rhythmic contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythmic_contemporary "Rhythmic contemporary") radio stations on November 12.[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) "[Like Him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Like_Him "Like Him")", featuring the British singer [Lola Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lola_Young_\(singer\) "Lola Young (singer)"), was released to rhythmic radio on February 11, 2025.[\[29\]](#cite_note-:02-29) A teaser for its eleventh track, "Thought I Was Dead", was shared on October 26.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](#cite_note-31) Three more songs were teased in a promotional video for the album's limited edition vinyl.[\[32\]](#cite_note-hype-32) On August 19, Tyler released the music video for "Darling, I".[\[33\]](#cite_note-33)

### Tour

Chromakopia: The World Tour was announced on October 23, 2024, with additional shows announced October 29, 2024.[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) Promoted by [AEG Presents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEG_Presents "AEG Presents"), the tour featured [Lil Yachty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Yachty "Lil Yachty") and [Paris Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Texas_\(hip-hop_group\) "Paris Texas (hip-hop group)") as supporting acts, with 53 dates across North America, including the U.S. and Canada, 24 dates in Western Europe and the UK, and 12 shows scheduled in Oceania, covering Australia and New Zealand.[\[35\]](#cite_note-variety_oct23-35) The tour took place throughout 2025 and concluded on September 21, 2025.

_Chromakopia_ was met with widespread critical acclaim. At [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a [normalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") rating out of 100 to reviews from professional publications, the album received an [average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean") score of 85, based on 17 reviews.[\[37\]](#cite_note-MC-37) Aggregator AnyDecentMusic? gave it 8.0 out of 10, based on their assessment of the critical consensus.[\[36\]](#cite_note-ADM-36)

Reviewing the album for [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), David Crone claimed that, "_Chromakopia_ is less of a cohesive statement than Tyler's fans are used to hearing; it's erratic and candid at once, a strange pressure cooker of boasts and doubts that falls out of step with its deftly sequenced and thematically tight predecessors."[\[38\]](#cite_note-AllMusic-38) Writing for _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_\(magazine\) "Clash (magazine)")_, Niall Smith wrote that "the project's mid-section advances the album's winning streak", however, "while there aren't any outright weak tracks" on the record, occasionally, "the pacing feels slightly less focused than Tyler's previous work". Smith concluded that "while some elements feel a bit safe, the sound design is chiseled and sharper" while noting that the album showcases Tyler's "now-mastered style in HD glory".[\[39\]](#cite_note-Clash-39) _[Consequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_\(publication\) "Consequence (publication)")_'s Jonah Krueger wrote that "the maternal presence is felt throughout the tracklist" and that Tyler "\[explores\] his anxieties and trauma" throughout the record.[\[40\]](#cite_note-cons-40) Writing for _Dork_, Jake Hawkes noted that _Chromakopia_ is a project "that bulges at the seams" and that "Tyler somehow wrangles it into something cohesive". Hawkes continued, "lyrically, Tyler seems at his most confessional in years", before concluding, stating that the album "has depth, it has worldbuilding, but just as importantly, it has some absolute bangers, too".[\[9\]](#cite_note-Dork-9)

_[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")_'s [Alexis Petridis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Petridis "Alexis Petridis") wrote that "tracks shift and slip their moorings, lurching from one sound to another" and that often, they change "completely over the course of a few minutes". Petridis concluded that "_Chromakopia_ ultimately seems to manifest a state of confusion, in which everything is in flux and nothing is quite as it initially seems".[\[42\]](#cite_note-The_Guardian-42) Steven Loftin for _[The Line of Best Fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Line_of_Best_Fit "The Line of Best Fit")_ wrote that "_Chromakopia_'s execution has been well thought out and finessed", however, "it is messy and it is truthful". Loftin expressed that the album "continues piecing together the Tyler, the Creator puzzle without making the picture any clearer".[\[6\]](#cite_note-TLOBF-6) Tom Breihan, writing for _[Stereogum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereogum "Stereogum")_, mentioned the album's similarity with Kendrick Lamar's album _[Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Morale_&_the_Big_Steppers "Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers")_ (2022), noting that _Chromakopia_ is "Tyler's therapy record, his self-conscious attempt to figure his shit out in full view of the public".[\[47\]](#cite_note-47) _Billboard_'s Mackenzie Cummings-Grady wrote that the album "contains something for everyone" and that "within this universal and at times nostalgic construction, the album is also incredibly reflective".[\[13\]](#cite_note-BB_songs_ranked-13)

Less enthusiastic reviews complained that the album's sound was too messy and chaotic. _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_'s Fred Garratt-Stanley regarded the album's sound as "deliberately messy" and the overall message about not trusting people as "lazy" but appreciated the themes and the honest and empathetic lyrics.[\[43\]](#cite_note-NME-43) _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_'s Paul Attard similarly criticized the album's sound and the "overworked" composition, saying that "Tyler's ambitions on _Chromakopia_ are grand, but the album attempts to do a lot while saying little".[\[46\]](#cite_note-Slant-46)

### Industry awards

## Commercial performance

Despite being released on Monday, _Chromakopia_ debuted at number one on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart with 299,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit") sold in its partial week along with 142,000 pure sales.[\[80\]](#cite_note-80) _Chromakopia_ surpassed _[Call Me If You Get Lost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_Me_If_You_Get_Lost "Call Me If You Get Lost")_ (169,000 units) as Tyler's biggest first week sales. The album also marked the biggest debut, by units, for a rap album released in 2024 at the time.[\[81\]](#cite_note-81)[\[82\]](#cite_note-82) The single "Noid" and the track "St. Chroma" peaked at number 10 and seven on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), respectively, marking his first top 10 hits on that chart.[\[83\]](#cite_note-83)

In _Chromakopia_'s second week, the album earned 160,000 equivalent album units in the United States, securing a second consecutive week at number one on the _Billboard_ 200 chart.[\[84\]](#cite_note-84) On the Hot 100, "Sticky" jumped to a new peak of number 10, having debuted at number 14. _**Chromakopia**_ (stylized in [all caps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_caps "All caps")) is the eighth studio album by the American rapper [Tyler, the Creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler,_the_Creator "Tyler, the Creator"). It was released through [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") on October 28, 2024, serving as the follow-up to _[Call Me If You Get Lost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_Me_If_You_Get_Lost "Call Me If You Get Lost")_ (2021). _Chromakopia_ was written, produced, and arranged by Tyler himself. The album features guest appearances from [Daniel Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Caesar "Daniel Caesar"), [Doechii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doechii "Doechii"), [GloRilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GloRilla "GloRilla"), LaToiya Williams, [Lil Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Wayne "Lil Wayne"), [Lola Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lola_Young_\(singer\) "Lola Young (singer)"), [Santigold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santigold "Santigold"), [Schoolboy Q](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoolboy_Q "Schoolboy Q"), [Sexyy Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexyy_Red "Sexyy Red"), and [Teezo Touchdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teezo_Touchdown "Teezo Touchdown"), with physical releases of the album additionally featuring [Playboi Carti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboi_Carti "Playboi Carti").

The album blends different genres like [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"), [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), and [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), evocative of Tyler's previous releases _[Flower Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower_Boy "Flower Boy")_ (2017) and _[Igor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igor_\(album\) "Igor (album)")_ (2019). Conceptually, _Chromakopia_ is narrated by Tyler's mother, Bonita Smith, as a [diary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary "Diary") that pieces together Tyler's perspective on past timeline experiences separated by tracks. The album received widespread acclaim from critics, who praised the lyricism, cohesiveness, and production, and even noted its messy and confusing nature as a positive.

_Chromakopia_ was supported by the singles "[Noid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noid_\(Tyler,_the_Creator_song\) "Noid (Tyler, the Creator song)")", "[Sticky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sticky_\(Tyler,_the_Creator_song\) "Sticky (Tyler, the Creator song)")", and "[Like Him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Like_Him "Like Him")", as well as the promotional singles "[St. Chroma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Chroma "St. Chroma")" and "[Thought I Was Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thought_I_Was_Dead "Thought I Was Dead")". The album was a commercial success, debuting at number one in nine countries. In the United States, the album debuted at the top of the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), earning Tyler his third US number-one album. Several other songs from the album also charted on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), such as "Noid" and "St. Chroma". At the [68th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/68th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "68th Annual Grammy Awards"), the album received nominations for [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year"), [Best Rap Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rap_Album "Grammy Award for Best Rap Album") and [Best Album Cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Album_Cover "Grammy Award for Best Album Cover"), in addition to "[Darling, I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darling,_I "Darling, I")" receiving a nomination for [Best Rap Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rap_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance") and "Sticky" for [Best Rap Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rap_Song "Grammy Award for Best Rap Song"). In support of the album, Tyler embarked on [Chromakopia: The World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromakopia:_The_World_Tour "Chromakopia: The World Tour") between February 2025 and March 2026.

## Background and recording

On October 28, 2024, during Tyler, the Creator's _Chromakopia_ exclusive listening event, Tyler revealed the meaning behind the album, noting that the album was originally about him growing up in [Hawthorne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawthorne,_California "Hawthorne, California"), [Inglewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inglewood,_California "Inglewood, California"). He revealed on stage that "no one knows anything about me from before I was like 17" and that the record turned into Tyler "taking a bunch of shit my mom told me as a kid."[\[1\]](#cite_note-Listening_Event_LA-1) Tyler uploaded a video on his official [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel titled "MASK IS OFF: CHROMAKOPIA" on November 12, 2024, which chronicles the creative process of the album, including [behind-the-scenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behind-the-scenes "Behind-the-scenes") clips from composition sessions, instrumentation arrangements and engineering work.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)

## Composition

### Music

Primarily a [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"), [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B"), and [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") album, _Chromakopia_ embraces [eclectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism "Eclecticism") instrumentation.[\[3\]](#cite_note-MEFeater-3) It blends musical styles reminiscent of Tyler's fourth and fifth albums _[Cherry Bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Bomb_\(album\) "Cherry Bomb (album)")_ (2015) and _[Flower Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower_Boy "Flower Boy")_ (2017), such as [neo soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo_soul "Neo soul") melodies and [synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer")\-based arrangements.[\[3\]](#cite_note-MEFeater-3) [Military cadences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_music "Martial music") and [soulful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") elements are also present on the album.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) This is Tyler's first album since his second studio album, _[Goblin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goblin_\(album\) "Goblin (album)")_, to not have the 10th track on the album feature multiple titles and parts.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

### Themes and lyrics

_Chromakopia_ is narrated by Tyler's mother, Bonita Smith.[\[6\]](#cite_note-TLOBF-6) Its [concept](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album") was inspired by his experience growing up in [Greater Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Los_Angeles "Greater Los Angeles") and the life lessons he learned from Smith as a child, that he began to understand and appreciate as he grew older.[\[7\]](#cite_note-Monogamy-7) Before the album's release, publications speculated that the album could be based on the story of Chroma the Great, a powerful [conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conducting "Conducting") whose orchestra creates the colors of the world, from the 1961 children's novel _[The Phantom Tollbooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Phantom_Tollbooth "The Phantom Tollbooth")_.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) _[Dork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dork_\(magazine\) "Dork (magazine)")_'s Jake Hawkes notes the character ties into the album's [aesthetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesthetics "Aesthetics"), but has little impact on the lyrical material.[\[9\]](#cite_note-Dork-9)

Smith describes him as the light and tells him to never dim his light for anyone.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) "[Rah Tah Tah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rah_Tah_Tah "Rah Tah Tah")" features [braggadocious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braggadocio_\(rap\) "Braggadocio (rap)") lyrics, as Tyler declares himself as the biggest rapper from Los Angeles after [Kendrick Lamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendrick_Lamar "Kendrick Lamar").[\[9\]](#cite_note-Dork-9) "[Noid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noid_\(Tyler,_the_Creator_song\) "Noid (Tyler, the Creator song)")", on the other hand, explores his anxieties with [celebrity culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_culture "Celebrity culture") and [parasocial relationships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasocial_relationships "Parasocial relationships").[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) In "[Darling, I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darling,_I "Darling, I")", featuring vocals by [Teezo Touchdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teezo_Touchdown "Teezo Touchdown"), Tyler reflects on his artistic ambition and the practice of [monogamy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monogamy "Monogamy").[\[7\]](#cite_note-Monogamy-7)

Titled after the [abortion-related healthcare company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey_Jane "Hey Jane"), "Hey Jane" stages a conversation between Tyler and an anonymous, older woman in the wake of an unplanned pregnancy.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_'s Mackenzie Cummings-Grady wrote that on the record, Tyler "speaks on his consuming paranoia" while narrating his "desire for children".[\[13\]](#cite_note-BB_songs_ranked-13)

Provoked by [Beyoncé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyoncé "Beyoncé")'s [surprise release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surprise_release "Surprise release") of her [2013 self-titled album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyoncé_\(album\) "Beyoncé (album)"),[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) the [International Federation of the Phonographic Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_the_Phonographic_Industry "International Federation of the Phonographic Industry") (IFPI) changed the day of the week when music is released worldwide from Tuesday to Friday.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) Tyler criticized the industry standard in a 2023 interview with [Nardwuar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nardwuar "Nardwuar"), suggesting that it promotes "passive listening".[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) He chose to release _Chromakopia_ on Monday, October 28, 2024, at 6 a.m. [ET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone").[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)

Trucks and [shipping containers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipping_container "Shipping container") promoting _Chromakopia_ were spotted in various cities across the U.S., including [Tyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler,_Texas "Tyler, Texas"), Houston, Dallas, Atlanta, [Charlotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte,_North_Carolina "Charlotte, North Carolina"), [Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"), Philadelphia, [Roswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell,_New_Mexico "Roswell, New Mexico"), Phoenix, Hawthorne (Tyler's hometown), and Los Angeles.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) Shortly after the video for "St. Chroma" released, the phone number +1 (855) 444–8888, which was previously used as promotion for _Call Me If You Get Lost_, was changed to a voicemail concerning the "Chromakopia Trucking Company", where a voice said that all the company's drivers were unavailable and to call later. One day before its release, Tyler held an album listening party at [Intuit Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intuit_Dome "Intuit Dome").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Listening_Event_LA-1)

A deluxe edition of the album, titled _Chromakopia+_, was released on October 29, 2025.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) It includes the bonus track "Mother", which was previously exclusive to the album's vinyl LP release.[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)

### Singles

On October 16, 2024, Tyler posted a teaser for _Chromakopia_'s opening track, "St. Chroma", on his [social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media "Social media") accounts.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) He revealed the album's name, release date, and [cover art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_art "Cover art") the following day.[\[24\]](#cite_note-variety_oct17-24)[\[25\]](#cite_note-25) The album's [lead single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single"), "Noid", was released on October 21.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) The following single, "[Sticky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sticky_\(Tyler,_the_Creator_song\) "Sticky (Tyler, the Creator song)")" featuring [GloRilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GloRilla "GloRilla"), [Sexyy Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexyy_Red "Sexyy Red"), and [Lil Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Wayne "Lil Wayne"), was released to [rhythmic contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythmic_contemporary "Rhythmic contemporary") radio stations on November 12.[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) "[Like Him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Like_Him "Like Him")", featuring the British singer [Lola Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lola_Young_\(singer\) "Lola Young (singer)"), was released to rhythmic radio on February 11, 2025.[\[29\]](#cite_note-:02-29) A teaser for its eleventh track, "Thought I Was Dead", was shared on October 26.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](#cite_note-31) Three more songs were teased in a promotional video for the album's limited edition vinyl.[\[32\]](#cite_note-hype-32) On August 19, Tyler released the music video for "Darling, I".[\[33\]](#cite_note-33)

### Tour

Chromakopia: The World Tour was announced on October 23, 2024, with additional shows announced October 29, 2024.[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) Promoted by [AEG Presents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEG_Presents "AEG Presents"), the tour featured [Lil Yachty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Yachty "Lil Yachty") and [Paris Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Texas_\(hip-hop_group\) "Paris Texas (hip-hop group)") as supporting acts, with 53 dates across North America, including the U.S. and Canada, 24 dates in Western Europe and the UK, and 12 shows scheduled in Oceania, covering Australia and New Zealand.[\[35\]](#cite_note-variety_oct23-35) The tour took place throughout 2025 and concluded on September 21, 2025.

_Chromakopia_ was met with widespread critical acclaim. At [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a [normalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") rating out of 100 to reviews from professional publications, the album received an [average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean") score of 85, based on 17 reviews.[\[37\]](#cite_note-MC-37) Aggregator AnyDecentMusic? gave it 8.0 out of 10, based on their assessment of the critical consensus.[\[36\]](#cite_note-ADM-36)

Reviewing the album for [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"), David Crone claimed that, "_Chromakopia_ is less of a cohesive statement than Tyler's fans are used to hearing; it's erratic and candid at once, a strange pressure cooker of boasts and doubts that falls out of step with its deftly sequenced and thematically tight predecessors."[\[38\]](#cite_note-AllMusic-38) Writing for _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_\(magazine\) "Clash (magazine)")_, Niall Smith wrote that "the project's mid-section advances the album's winning streak", however, "while there aren't any outright weak tracks" on the record, occasionally, "the pacing feels slightly less focused than Tyler's previous work". Smith concluded that "while some elements feel a bit safe, the sound design is chiseled and sharper" while noting that the album showcases Tyler's "now-mastered style in HD glory".[\[39\]](#cite_note-Clash-39) _[Consequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_\(publication\) "Consequence (publication)")_'s Jonah Krueger wrote that "the maternal presence is felt throughout the tracklist" and that Tyler "\[explores\] his anxieties and trauma" throughout the record.[\[40\]](#cite_note-cons-40) Writing for _Dork_, Jake Hawkes noted that _Chromakopia_ is a project "that bulges at the seams" and that "Tyler somehow wrangles it into something cohesive". Hawkes continued, "lyrically, Tyler seems at his most confessional in years", before concluding, stating that the album "has depth, it has worldbuilding, but just as importantly, it has some absolute bangers, too".[\[9\]](#cite_note-Dork-9)

_[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")_'s [Alexis Petridis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Petridis "Alexis Petridis") wrote that "tracks shift and slip their moorings, lurching from one sound to another" and that often, they change "completely over the course of a few minutes". Petridis concluded that "_Chromakopia_ ultimately seems to manifest a state of confusion, in which everything is in flux and nothing is quite as it initially seems".[\[42\]](#cite_note-The_Guardian-42) Steven Loftin for _[The Line of Best Fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Line_of_Best_Fit "The Line of Best Fit")_ wrote that "_Chromakopia_'s execution has been well thought out and finessed", however, "it is messy and it is truthful". Loftin expressed that the album "continues piecing together the Tyler, the Creator puzzle without making the picture any clearer".[\[6\]](#cite_note-TLOBF-6) Tom Breihan, writing for _[Stereogum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereogum "Stereogum")_, mentioned the album's similarity with Kendrick Lamar's album _[Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Morale_&_the_Big_Steppers "Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers")_ (2022), noting that _Chromakopia_ is "Tyler's therapy record, his self-conscious attempt to figure his shit out in full view of the public".[\[47\]](#cite_note-47) _Billboard_'s Mackenzie Cummings-Grady wrote that the album "contains something for everyone" and that "within this universal and at times nostalgic construction, the album is also incredibly reflective".[\[13\]](#cite_note-BB_songs_ranked-13)

Less enthusiastic reviews complained that the album's sound was too messy and chaotic. _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_'s Fred Garratt-Stanley regarded the album's sound as "deliberately messy" and the overall message about not trusting people as "lazy" but appreciated the themes and the honest and empathetic lyrics.[\[43\]](#cite_note-NME-43) _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_'s Paul Attard similarly criticized the album's sound and the "overworked" composition, saying that "Tyler's ambitions on _Chromakopia_ are grand, but the album attempts to do a lot while saying little".[\[46\]](#cite_note-Slant-46)

### Industry awards

## Commercial performance

Despite being released on Monday, _Chromakopia_ debuted at number one on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart with 299,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit") sold in its partial week along with 142,000 pure sales.[\[80\]](#cite_note-80) _Chromakopia_ surpassed _[Call Me If You Get Lost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_Me_If_You_Get_Lost "Call Me If You Get Lost")_ (169,000 units) as Tyler's biggest first week sales. The album also marked the biggest debut, by units, for a rap album released in 2024 at the time.[\[81\]](#cite_note-81)[\[82\]](#cite_note-82) The single "Noid" and the track "St. Chroma" peaked at number 10 and seven on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), respectively, marking his first top 10 hits on that chart.[\[83\]](#cite_note-83)

# Shaboozey’s ‘A Bar Song (Tipsy)’ Ties Decade’s Longest Hot 100 Rule With 16th Week at No. 1

Plus, Lady Gaga & Bruno Mars' "Die With a Smile" hits a new No. 2 high and Tyler, the Creator notches his first two top 10s.

11/4/2024

[Shaboozey](https://www.billboard.com/artist/shaboozey/)’s “A Bar Song (Tipsy)” rebounds a spot for a 16th week at No. 1 on the [Billboard Hot 100](https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100), matching the longest reign of the 2020s. The song, which became the singer-songwriter’s [first leader](https://www.billboard.com/lists/shaboozey-chappell-roan-hot-100-top-10/) in July, matches the domination of Morgan Wallen’s “Last Night” – like “A Bar Song (Tipsy),” a country-pop crossover smash – in 2023.

Over the Hot 100’s entire 66-year history, “A Bar Song (Tipsy)” is now tied for the second-longest command, among just five hits to have led for at least 16 weeks. Lil Nas X’s “Old Town Road,” featuring Billy Ray Cyrus, ruled for a record 19 weeks in 2019.

“A Bar Song (Tipsy)” additionally extends the longest No. 1 run this year – 20 weeks – on the multimetric [Hot Country Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/country-songs/) chart. It’s one of only nine titles to reach the milestone since the survey became the genre’s all-encompassing songs chart in 1958.

Elsewhere in the Hot 100’s top 10, [Lady Gaga](https://www.billboard.com/artist/lady-gaga/) and [Bruno Mars](https://www.billboard.com/artist/bruno-mars/)’ “Die With a Smile” rises 4-2 for a new high, aided by three new versions and sale-pricing during the tracking week.

Plus, [Tyler, the Creator](https://www.billboard.com/artist/tyler-the-creator/) notches his first two Hot 100 top 10s: “St. Chroma,” featuring [Daniel Caesar](https://www.billboard.com/artist/daniel-caesar/) – the week’s most-streamed song – debuts at No. 7 and “Noid” soars 43-10. Both are from his new album, _Chromakopia_, which [launches at No. 1](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/tyler-the-creator-chromakopia-debuts-no-1-billboard-200-1235818700/) on the [Billboard 200](https://www.billboard.com/charts/billboard-200/) chart.

The Hot 100 blends all-genre U.S. streaming (official audio and official video), radio airplay and sales data, the lattermost metric reflecting purchases of physical singles and digital tracks from full-service digital music retailers; digital singles sales from direct-to-consumer (D2C) sites are excluded from chart calculations. All charts (dated Nov. 9, 2024) will update on Billboard.com Tuesday, Nov. 5). For all chart news, you can follow @billboard and @billboardcharts on both X, formerly known as Twitter, and Instagram.

_Luminate, the independent data provider to the_ Billboard _charts, completes a thorough review of all data submissions used in compiling the weekly chart rankings. Luminate reviews and authenticates data. In partnership with_ Billboard_, data deemed suspicious or unverifiable is removed, using established criteria, before final chart calculations are made and published._

*   ## ‘Tipsy’ Airplay, Streams & Sales
    
    “A Bar Song (Tipsy),” on American Dogwood/EMPIRE (with country radio promotion by Magnolia Music), totaled 72.6 million radio airplay audience impressions (up 1% week-over-week), 22.1 million official streams (down 8%) and 5,000 sold (down 19%) in the United States Oct. 25-31.
    
    The track holds for a 14th week at No. 1 on [Radio Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/radio-songs/) and drops 3-7 after 14 weeks atop [Digital Song Sales](https://www.billboard.com/charts/digital-song-sales/) and 3-8 following nine weeks atop [Streaming Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/streaming-songs).
    
*   ## Hits With the Most Weeks at No. 1 All-Time
    
    “A Bar Song (Tipsy)” equals the 16-week Hot 100 reign of Morgan Wallen’s “Last Night” in 2023 for the longest of the 2020s. (The former breaks out of a tie with Harry Styles’ 15-week leader “As It Was” in 2022.)
    
    “A Bar Song (Tipsy)” is now one of only five No. 1s in the Hot 100’s entire history to amass 16 or more weeks on top – of 1,175 total leaders dating to the chart’s Aug. 4, 1958, start. (All five have led since the chart adopted electronically monitored Luminate data in November 1991, at which point longer reigns than before subsequently became more common.)
    
    Here’s a recap of the five [longest-leading Hot 100 No. 1s](https://www.billboard.com/pro/hot-100-songs-longest-leading-no-1s/) over the chart’s history:
    
    *   19 weeks, “Old Town Road,” Lil Nas X feat. Billy Ray Cyrus, 2019
    *   16 (to date), “A Bar Song (Tipsy),” Shaboozey, 2024
    *   16, “Last Night,” Morgan Wallen, 2023
    *   16, “Despacito,” Luis Fonsi & Daddy Yankee feat. Justin Bieber, 2017
    *   16, “One Sweet Day,” Mariah Carey & Boyz II Men, 1995-96
    
*   ## New Reason to ‘Smile’
    
    ![Lady Gaga & Bruno Mars](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/lady-gaga-bruno-mars-press-credit-John-Esparza-2024-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: John Esparza
    
    Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars’ “Die With a Smile” pushes 4-2 for a new Hot 100 high (outpacing its prior No. 3 peak reached upon its debut in late August), aided by three new versions, which, like the original mix, were discounted to 69 cents in the iTunes Store during the tracking week. “Live in Las Vegas” and instrumental versions were released Oct. 29, followed by an acoustic version Oct. 31.
    
    The song (with all versions combined for charting and data tracking purposes) drew 45.3 million in radio reach (up 9%) and 22.6 million streams (up nearly 1%) and sold 16,000 (up 329%) Oct. 25-31. It rebounds for a second week at No. 1 on Digital Song Sales, while rising 11-9 on Radio Songs, where it becomes Mars’ 19th top 10 and Gaga’s 12th. The ballad marks her first Radio Songs top 10 this decade and her highest rank since “Applause” reached No. 7 in 2013.
    
*   ## Tyler’s Two New Top 10s
    
    ![Tyler The Creator 2024](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/tyler-the-creator-cr-luis-panch-perez-2024-press-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Luis “Panch” Perez
    
    Tyler, the Creator claims his first two Hot 100 top 10s: “St. Chroma,” featuring Daniel Caesar, debuts at No. 7 and “Noid” surges 43-10. The songs reach the region almost entirely from streaming, with 24.3 million and 23.2 million streams, respectively. Notably, the former was released Oct. 28 and logs its sum from just four days during the tracking week; the latter drew 10.6 million streams in the prior tracking week, also over four days, following its Oct. 21 release. “St. Chroma” concurrently debuts as Tyler, the Creator’s first No. 1 on Streaming Songs.
    
    Prior to this week, Tyler, the Creator charted 33 Hot 100 titles, hitting a No. 13 high with “Earfquake” in 2019. His new entries are from his album _Chromakopia_, which [premieres at No. 1](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/tyler-the-creator-chromakopia-debuts-no-1-billboard-200-1235818700/) on the Billboard 200, where it’s his third leader.
    
    Caesar scores his second Hot 100 top 10 and Streaming Songs No. 1: Justin Bieber’s “Peaches,” on which he and Giveon are featured, led each list for a week in April 2021.
    
*   ## Rest of the Top 10: ‘Birds of a Feather’ & More
    
    Billie Eilish’s “Birds of a Feather” holds at No. 3 on the Hot 100 after reaching No. 2. It tops the multimetric [Hot Rock & Alternative Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/rock-songs/) and [Hot Alternative Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-alternative-songs/) charts for a 13th week each.
    
    Sabrina Carpenter’s “Espresso” rises 5-4 on the Hot 100, after hitting No. 3, while her “Taste” is steady at No. 9, after it debuted at its No. 2 high.
    
    Post Malone’s “I Had Some Help,” featuring Morgan Wallen, ascends 6-5 on the Hot 100, following [six weeks at No. 1](https://www.billboard.com/lists/post-malone-morgan-wallen-i-had-some-help-hot-100-number-one-debut/) beginning upon its debut in May.
    
    Teddy Swims’ “Lose Control,” which led the Hot 100 for a [week in March](https://www.billboard.com/lists/teddy-swims-lose-control-number-one-hot-100/), lifts 7-6 – and solely claims the third-most weeks spent in the top 10 all-time:
    
    *   57 weeks, “Blinding Lights,” The Weeknd, 2020-21
    *   44, “Stay,” The Kid Laroi & Justin Bieber, 2021-22
    *   42 (to date), “Lose Control,” Teddy Swims, 2024
    *   41, “Last Night,” Morgan Wallen, 2023-24
    *   41, “Levitating,” Dua Lipa, 2021
    
    Also in the Hot 100’s top 10, Wallen’s “Love Somebody” falls to No. 8, a week after it [debuted](https://www.billboard.com/lists/morgan-wallen-love-somebody-hot-100-number-one-debut/) as his third No. 1.

*   ## New Reason to ‘Smile’
    
    ![Lady Gaga & Bruno Mars](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/lady-gaga-bruno-mars-press-credit-John-Esparza-2024-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: John Esparza
    
    Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars’ “Die With a Smile” pushes 4-2 for a new Hot 100 high (outpacing its prior No. 3 peak reached upon its debut in late August), aided by three new versions, which, like the original mix, were discounted to 69 cents in the iTunes Store during the tracking week. “Live in Las Vegas” and instrumental versions were released Oct. 29, followed by an acoustic version Oct. 31.
    
    The song (with all versions combined for charting and data tracking purposes) drew 45.3 million in radio reach (up 9%) and 22.6 million streams (up nearly 1%) and sold 16,000 (up 329%) Oct. 25-31. It rebounds for a second week at No. 1 on Digital Song Sales, while rising 11-9 on Radio Songs, where it becomes Mars’ 19th top 10 and Gaga’s 12th. The ballad marks her first Radio Songs top 10 this decade and her highest rank since “Applause” reached No. 7 in 2013.
    
*   ## Tyler’s Two New Top 10s
    
    ![Tyler The Creator 2024](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/tyler-the-creator-cr-luis-panch-perez-2024-press-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Luis “Panch” Perez
    
    Tyler, the Creator claims his first two Hot 100 top 10s: “St. Chroma,” featuring Daniel Caesar, debuts at No. 7 and “Noid” surges 43-10. The songs reach the region almost entirely from streaming, with 24.3 million and 23.2 million streams, respectively. Notably, the former was released Oct. 28 and logs its sum from just four days during the tracking week; the latter drew 10.6 million streams in the prior tracking week, also over four days, following its Oct. 21 release. “St. Chroma” concurrently debuts as Tyler, the Creator’s first No. 1 on Streaming Songs.
    
    Prior to this week, Tyler, the Creator charted 33 Hot 100 titles, hitting a No. 13 high with “Earfquake” in 2019. His new entries are from his album _Chromakopia_, which [premieres at No. 1](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/tyler-the-creator-chromakopia-debuts-no-1-billboard-200-1235818700/) on the Billboard 200, where it’s his third leader.
    
    Caesar scores his second Hot 100 top 10 and Streaming Songs No. 1: Justin Bieber’s “Peaches,” on which he and Giveon are featured, led each list for a week in April 2021.
    
*   ## Rest of the Top 10: ‘Birds of a Feather’ & More
    
    Billie Eilish’s “Birds of a Feather” holds at No. 3 on the Hot 100 after reaching No. 2. It tops the multimetric [Hot Rock & Alternative Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/rock-songs/) and [Hot Alternative Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-alternative-songs/) charts for a 13th week each.
    
    Sabrina Carpenter’s “Espresso” rises 5-4 on the Hot 100, after hitting No. 3, while her “Taste” is steady at No. 9, after it debuted at its No. 2 high.
    
    Post Malone’s “I Had Some Help,” featuring Morgan Wallen, ascends 6-5 on the Hot 100, following [six weeks at No. 1](https://www.billboard.com/lists/post-malone-morgan-wallen-i-had-some-help-hot-100-number-one-debut/) beginning upon its debut in May.
    
    Teddy Swims’ “Lose Control,” which led the Hot 100 for a [week in March](https://www.billboard.com/lists/teddy-swims-lose-control-number-one-hot-100/), lifts 7-6 – and solely claims the third-most weeks spent in the top 10 all-time:
    
    *   57 weeks, “Blinding Lights,” The Weeknd, 2020-21
    *   44, “Stay,” The Kid Laroi & Justin Bieber, 2021-22
    *   42 (to date), “Lose Control,” Teddy Swims, 2024
    *   41, “Last Night,” Morgan Wallen, 2023-24
    *   41, “Levitating,” Dua Lipa, 2021
    
    Also in the Hot 100’s top 10, Wallen’s “Love Somebody” falls to No. 8, a week after it [debuted](https://www.billboard.com/lists/morgan-wallen-love-somebody-hot-100-number-one-debut/) as his third No. 1.

## About Tyler, The Creator

Tyler, the Creator has evolved from an underground provocateur into one of the most creatively influential artists in modern hip-hop, who’s known for fusing jazz, soul, funk, and alternative rap into richly self-produced albums. Beginning with the cult success of _Goblin_ and the rebellious energy of Odd Future, his wide-spanning music collective, Tyler expanded his artistic range through critically acclaimed projects such as _Flower Boy_, _IGOR_, and _Call Me If You Get Lost_, collectively spawning standout tracks like “EARFQUAKE,” “See You Again,” and “WUSYANAME.” His genre-defying work has earned him multiple Grammy wins and Grammy nominations, while _IGOR_ in particular redefined expectations for mainstream rap albums by centering melody, emotional vulnerability, and intricate arrangements over conventional hip-hop structures. Beyond music, Tyler has built a global creative brand through fashion, visual direction, and live performance aesthetics, helping normalize eccentric individuality and auteur-style artistic control within contemporary rap culture. A lesser-known detail that longtime fans appreciate is that Tyler taught himself piano production techniques largely by ear and often layers synths inspired by artists like [Pharrell Williams](https://www.grammy.com/artists/pharrell-williams/7310/) and [Stevie Wonder](https://www.grammy.com/artists/stevie-wonder/8257/), which contributes to the warm, cinematic textures that distinguish his later albums from his early lo-fi sound.

# Tyler, the Creator's 'Chromakopia' Album: Features and Credits

[Tyler, the Creator](https://www.complex.com/music/a/tracewilliamcowen/tyler-the-creator-album-release-date) has set the tone for the rest of the week, if not the months ahead, with the fuck-a-Friday rollout of his new album [_Chromakopia_](https://www.complex.com/music/a/tracewilliamcowen/tyler-the-creator-chromakopia).

As has long been the case with Tyler releases, _Chromakopia_ sees the two-time Best Rap Album winner [welcoming fans into a whole new world](https://www.complex.com/music/a/tracewilliamcowen/tyler-the-creator-chromakopia-noid-video-ayo-edebiri) by way of a carefully crafted, rewardingly layered, and inspiringly vulnerable central narrative. The production here, expectedly, is truly out-of-this-world great, providing the album with an impenetrability that also extends to its shrewd sequencing decisions. On first listen, the transitions are seamless, and each song feels as though it’s speaking to its counterparts from across the album’s 53-minute runtime.

The album is [written, produced, and arrange](https://www.instagram.com/p/DBOvKSFvDFQ/?hl=en)d by Tyler. For a deeper look into the credits (as adapted from Spotify) and the not-initially-listed-on-streaming assortment of features, see below, but only if you’ve already embarked on your own inaugural listening experience. Otherwise, what follows could be said to contain spoilers. Proceed with caution.

**“St. Chroma” f/ Daniel Caesar**

Written by: Ashton Dumar Simmonds, Tyler Okonma

Produced by: Tyler, the Creator

**“Rah Tah Tah”**

Written by: Tyler Okonma

Produced by: Tyler, the Creator

**“Noid”**

Written by: Paul Dobson Nyirongo, Tyler Okonma

Produced by: Tyler, the Creator

**“Darling, I” f/ Teezo Touchdown**

Written by: Barry White, Kamaal Ibn John Fareed, Tyler Okonma

Produced by: Tyler, the Creator

**“Hey Jane”**

Written by: Tyler Okonma

Produced by: Tyler, the Creator

**“I Killed You”**

Written by: Tyler Okonma

Produced by: Tyler, the Creator

**“Judge Judy”**

Written by: Tyler Okonma

Produced by: Tyler, the Creator

**“Sticky” f/ GloRilla, Sexyy Red, and Lil Wayne**

Written by: Aaron Bolton, David Darnell Brown, Dudley Alexander Duverne, Dwyane Carter, Jr., Elvis L. Jr. Williams, Gloria Woods, Jamal F Jones, Janae Wherry, Rex Zamor, Tim Mosley, Timothy clayton, Tyler Okonma, Zachary Anson Wallace

Produced by: Tyler, the Creator

**“Take Your Mask Off” f/ Daniel Caesar & Latoiya Williams**

Written by: Greg CookK. Thomas, Tyler Okonma

Written by: Ashton Dumar Simmonds, Tyler Okonma

# Tyler, the Creator talks IGOR, Odd Future, and more in new 52-minute interview

July 18, 2019

[Tyler, the Creator](http://www.thefader.com/artist/tyler-the-creator)'s latest album _IGOR_ united fans and critics alike with its excellent production, and unprecedented vulnerability from the onetime Odd Future bandleader. That new project is the main focus of Tyler's new 52-minute interview with Beats 1's Zane Lowe for Apple Music, streaming above.

In the interview, Tyler explains how _IGOR_ became his most successful culmination of a lifelong approach to music. "Since day one, I've always wanted to make the prettiest shit that's borderline boring, or the hardest fucking shit," Tyler says. "And I've been trying to mix those together since my first album."

Tyler also touches on his relationship to his music pre-_Flower Boy_, which saw him lean more heavily on his talents as a songwriter and composer. "If I started at _Flower Boy_, and then \[_IGOR_\], I would be a god," he says. "I didn't realize I should stop yelling on songs until I was 24."

Watch the full interview above.

# Tyler, the Creator’s Anxieties About Fame Are Starting to Feel Universal

Chromokopia

On his latest single, a familiar refrain about modern celebrity culture strikes closer to home

Tyler, the Creator is speaking to the times on “NOID,” the newest single from his upcoming album, _Chromokopia_. The song is part of Tyler’s straight-to-the-point album rollout, where the music and visuals — not his characteristic outspokenness — have taken center stage. 

Last week, Tyler dropped “St. Chroma,” which featured him whispering over militaristic stomps. A week later, he dropped “NOID,” admitting he was “paranoid” about how stardom made him a target. “I can’t even buy a home in private/home invasion got my brothers dyin’,” he raps about the ever-present threat of celebrity burglaries.  

The black-and-white video serves to hammer Tyler’s consternation home. He flails about in a dark void, is chased by autograph-seeking fans, and has a frantic, gun-toting Ayo Ebidiri run up on him. The self-directed video offers almost three minutes of visuals for fans to decipher frame by frame. And likely before their analysis is done — or before he reveals all at his upcoming album-listening event — _Chromokopia_ will be here.

The short runway to his new album is becoming Tyler’s trademark. The Dissect Podcast’s official X account [pointed out that](https://twitter.com/dissectpodcast/status/1846586830512357857?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw%7Ctwcamp%5Etweetembed%7Ctwterm%5E1846586830512357857%7Ctwgr%5E%7Ctwcon%5Es1_&ref_url=) 2019’s _IGOR_ dropped 10 days after his rollout began, and 2021’s _Call Me If You Get Lost_ dropped 11 days after the first announcement. _Chromokopia_ is slated to drop 12 days after “St. Chroma.” It’s surprising that quietly dropping music feels like a unique rollout, but the music industry has made publicity stunts feel like a prerequisite for new releases: In 2024 alone, we’ve seen more prerelease beef than Midwest farms. Nonetheless, Tyler reminds us that there’s no need for cheap promo when your fan base just wants the music. 

He’s been open that he doesn’t think we need to know anything else anyway. In August, [he lamented to Maverick Carter](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/tyler-the-creator-fans-invading-privacy-1235080201/), “The internet’s crazy, these kids hack everything … they wanna know who your sister is, what you ate for dinner … mind your fuckin’ business. Go the fuck outside and listen to the damn art or the music. Because of the internet, people don’t know personal boundaries anymore, and it’s normalized … \[but\] it’s like ‘we don’t know each other.’” And here comes an album with a lead single with a Ngozi family sample that apparently translates to, “When you come to my house, please be respectful. Because I don’t like talking too much. Talking too much breeds gossip.” At least he’s consistent.

## Editor’s picks

While many theories abound, some fans believe the _Chromokopia_ album cover is a visual reference to David Bowie’s _“Heroes”_ album. Before the term “album era” was a thing, Bowie was revered for adopting different personas for each album. Tyler has done the same and presents his creative choices in layers for _Chromokopia_. In 1977, Bowie [told _NME_](https://www.rocksbackpages.com/Library/Article/david-bowie-who-was-that-unmasked-man) that the title in quotations on his album cover serves to “indicate a dimension of irony about the word ‘heroes’ or about the whole concept of heroism” — an idea that Tyler could be redressing as a commentary on celebrity worship. Bowie’s cover is a call to artist Erich Heckel’s painting _Roquairol,_ which British outlet [_Why Now_ described](https://whynow.co.uk/read/sex-drugs-and-roquairol-david-bowie-and-the-haunting-influence-of-german-expressionism-on-heroes) as “a disturbing portrait of artist Ernst Ludwig Kirchner in a state of nervous collapse.” Again, _Roquairol_’s tension, referenced by Bowie, also works on “NOID,” with Tyler venting, “Nervous system is shook, way before 19.”

## Trending Stories

Bowie’s biographer interprets that the _“Heroes”_ cover shows the singer “raising a flat palm as though he has just mimetically lifted the final mask of artifice from his face.” But instead of holding a mask, Tyler is wearing a brown leather mask. His veil could be fairly interpreted as a reference to the charade of modern celebrity. The mask _looks lik_e Tyler, but it’s a slight variation concocted to conceal his true identity. The song title, “NOID,” further hints that to the world, he’s not the Tyler Okonma that his family knows. He’s whatever character someone imagines him as. Like he told Carter, we don’t know him. 

“NOID” isn’t the first instance of a rapper pushing back against celebrity overexposure; one can look to Cardi B’s _Invasion of Privacy_ or Eminem’s “The Way I Am,” for instance. But the arrival of “NOID” dovetails with an influx of fans starting to agree with him that the modern construct of celebrity is unhealthy. Whether fans are pondering the power networks that enabled Diddy’s monstrous allegations or rolling their eyes at Trump-supporting stars, we’re all starting to agree with Kanye West, one of Tyler’s idols, that “no one man should have all that power.” Tyler agrees from inside the celebrity bubble, following up his previous comments about overzealous fans with a single that examines the weight of artists being treated like “Heroes.”
